newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Erste says Creditanstalt talks mired in problems.
newsitem.headline: Erste says Creditanstalt talks mired in problems.

text.p: Savings bank Die Erste said on Friday it still had to remove some major obstacles in negotiations with its partners before the consortium could make a final bid for government sell-off candidate Creditanstalt.
"Even though we have made good progress in our talks, some major issues are still open and there is no agreement so far," a spokesman for Die Erste Oesterreichische Spar-Casse Bank AG told Reuters.
Die Erste originally proposed to set up a joint holding company for Creditanstalt and planned to transfer 74.9 percent of its shares into the holding, which would hold all of Creditanstalt's capital.

The consortium, billed as the "Austrian solution" in the six-year long Creditanstalt privatisation saga, comprises insurer insurer EA-Generali AG, Germany's Commerzbank AG, Banca Commerciale Italiana SpA and several smaller Austrian companies, including a beverage maker.
The spokesman said the major disagreements within the consortium were over Die Erste's exact weight in the proposed holding company and how voting power would be distributed between its constituents.
"Because Die Erste is the Austrian bank partner in this consortium we feel we have a special responsibility," the spokesman said without elaborating further.

The bank said it was now proposing to increase its weight in the proposed holding. "We are now offering to put in a substantial amount of cash in order to safeguard Austrian interests," the spokesman said without giving further details.

Creditanstalt executives have privately rejected Die Erste's plans because they fear it would give the savings bank undue influence over Creditanstalt, with assets of almost 700 billion schillings ($67.2 billion) Austria's second-largest bank. Die Erste is less than a third the size of Creditanstalt.

Die Erste, which together with its partners is the only known bidder for the government's 70 percent voting stake in the bank, earlier said it was unable to comply with Finance Minister Viktor Klima's deadline to submit a final offer on Friday.

The government has long said it wanted to sell its stake in Creditanstalt in a way that safeguarded Austrian interests. Several international bidders over the past years have dropped their interest in the bank because of what they saw as a bias against foreigners in Austria's leading political circles. ($ = 10.41 Austrian Schillings)
